home.title: Submarine – free SSH, SFTP and FTP client with RDP and VNC
home.description: Free, open-source SSH, SFTP and FTP client with RDP, VNC and Telnet, for Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. Encrypted, with an optional AI assistant.

hero.pill: Remote desktops, FTP and an AI assistant
hero.title: All your servers in one encrypted app
hero.lede: Submarine is an SSH, SFTP, FTP, RDP, VNC and Telnet client for Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. Your servers, passwords and keys are encrypted on your device, and they sync between your devices only if you want them to.

remote.title: Remote desktops, right next to your terminals
remote.lede: VNC and the built-in RDP client open in a tab, directly or through one of your SSH servers. RDP can also open in your computer's own RDP app.

points.title: See how the link is doing
points.text: A mark in the tab says Good, Fair, Weak or Not answering, with the delay. Its panel shows how much data goes each way, and on a weak link it offers to use less data.

points.title: A sharp picture, or less data
points.text: Choose the colours, the resolution and, for VNC, how often the picture is updated, or pick a quick choice such as Less data. A hidden tab pauses its picture, so nothing is sent while nobody is looking.

points.title: A shared clipboard
points.text: Text you copy on the remote desktop comes to your clipboard, and yours goes there only when you paste. VNC carries plain text only.

points.title: Shared files over RDP
points.text: The built-in RDP client can share a folder or a whole drive, read only if you like. On a computer, not on a phone. The choice stays on this device and is never synced.

points.title: Your RDP app, without typing the password
points.text: Through an SSH server, your RDP app connects to the same local address every time, so what it remembers (a trusted certificate, a saved login) is found again. On Windows, Remote Desktop Connection also gets the saved password, encrypted, in a file that is deleted once it is read.

points.title: Through your SSH servers
points.text: RDP, VNC and Telnet can all go through one of your SSH servers. Connections that are not encrypted are clearly marked.

remote.alt: A remote desktop over RDP in a Submarine tab, with Paste, the connection mark (Good, 6 ms), Files and Settings in its bar
remote.altVnc: A VNC desktop in a Submarine tab, marked as not encrypted
remote.altSettings: The Speed and quality panel of a remote desktop tab
remote.note: The built-in RDP client is experimental, and off until you choose it for a server (Open in: Submarine's tab). Until then, RDP opens in your computer's RDP app. On Android, the built-in client is the one used.

ai.title: An AI assistant that asks first
ai.lede: Off until you set it up, and with the AI provider you choose. It looks into a server for you, changes files and runs commands, as far as the level you set allows.

points.title: Your own provider
points.text: Anthropic, OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible service such as OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq or Google Gemini, or a model on your own computer through Ollama or LM Studio. Requests go straight from the app to the provider.

points.title: In every session
points.text: An AI tab in each SSH and FTP session, and an AI page with all your chats. A chat can switch to another model or provider midway.

points.title: Reads, edits and runs
points.text: It reads files and folders, writes and edits files, and runs commands on SSH servers. The AI terminal shows each command and its output as it runs. On an FTP server it works with files only.

points.title: You choose how far it goes
points.text: Five levels for each server, from Suggest only to Full access. At the default, Ask, commands the app can tell only read run by themselves, and the rest wait for your OK. Every file change is listed in Activity and can be undone there.

points.title: It asks before sending
points.text: Before your first message goes to a provider, the app asks, and names where it goes. A private key in a command's output or in a file is removed before anything is sent. Provider keys and chats are kept encrypted on your device and are never synced.

points.title: AI agents on your computer
points.text: Claude Code and other agents that speak MCP can use your servers through Submarine, once you turn it on in Settings → AI agents. An agent asks for access, and you choose the server, the operations, the folders and for how long. It never gets a password, a key or the server's address.

ai.note: The screens of the AI assistant and the AI agents are in English for now.

privacy.title: Your data is yours. We can't read it.
privacy.lede: Your data is encrypted before it is saved, and before it leaves your device. We publish exactly what our server can and cannot see.

items.title: Encrypted on your device
items.text: Profiles are encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The key is made from your password with Argon2id. The password itself is never stored or sent.

items.title: Sync is optional
items.text: If you turn it on, every item is encrypted on your device first. The server keeps only the encrypted version. It does see some details around it, such as your email address and when you sync, and we list them all.

items.title: No tracking
items.text: No ads, no analytics, no crash reports. The app talks only to your servers, to the sync server if you sign in, to GitHub to check for a new version, to us when you send feedback, and to an AI provider only if you add one and use the assistant.

free.text: No paid plan, no trial, no ads, and no account needed.
items: Submarine is free and open source under the MIT license.
You don't need an account. An account is only for the optional sync between your devices.
The sync service is free as well, within fair limits: {limitMb} MB of encrypted data, {limitItems} items and {limitProfiles} profiles per account.
The source code of the app and of the sync server is public. You can read it, build the app yourself, or run a sync server of your own.

items.a: Yes. The app is free and open source under the MIT license, with no paid plan and no ads. The sync service is free too, within the limits above.
No. Everything works without one. You only need an account if you want to sync profiles between your devices.

items.q: Can the sync server read my passwords?
items.a: No. Every item is encrypted on your device before it is uploaded, and the server never gets the key. It does see some details around your data, such as your email address, when you sync, and how many items you have. The security page lists all of them.

items.q: What if I forget my profile password?
items.a: Then nobody can open that profile, not even us. There is no recovery, because the password is never stored anywhere. Keep it somewhere safe.

items.q: Can I use RDP, VNC and Telnet?
items.a: Yes, from version 0.5. VNC shows the screen in a tab and shares the clipboard (plain text). RDP opens in your computer's RDP app, or in a tab with the experimental built-in client, which shares the clipboard and, on a computer, a folder or a drive. In a Submarine tab, both show how the connection is doing and let you trade picture quality for less data. Telnet opens in a terminal tab. All three can go through an SSH server, and Telnet and plain VNC are marked as not encrypted.

items.q: Can I use FTP or FTPS?
items.a: Yes, from version 0.5. An FTP server opens in a tab with the same file browser as SFTP, with FTPS (TLS) by default, directly, through an SSH server or through a proxy. Plain FTP is there if you choose it, and the app says it isn't encrypted.

items.q: Does Submarine have an AI assistant?
items.a: Yes, from version 0.5, and it is off until you set it up in Settings → AI Assistant. It uses your own AI provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible service, or a local model through Ollama or LM Studio) and works on a server from that session's AI tab, at the level you choose. Nothing goes to a provider until you add one, agree, and send a message.

items.q: Can Claude Code or another AI agent use my servers through Submarine?
items.a: Yes, on a computer, from version 0.5. Turn it on in Settings → AI agents, which shows how to add Submarine to the agent (it speaks MCP). The agent asks for access, and you choose the server, the operations, the folders and the time. It never gets a password, a key or the server's address.

items.q: What does a remote desktop get from my computer?
items.a: Clipboard text when you paste into its tab, and nothing before that. Text copied on the server comes to your clipboard while Share the clipboard is on. Files only if you choose a folder or a drive for the built-in RDP client, on a computer. These choices are kept on your device and never synced, so nobody you share a profile with can turn them on.

items.q: Which systems does it run on?
items.a: Windows 10 and 11, macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 and later) and, from version 0.5, on Intel Macs, Linux (.deb, .rpm, Arch, AppImage) and Android 7.0 or later. For iPhone and iPad (iOS 15 or later), there is a beta on TestFlight.

items.q: Which languages is the app in?
items.a: From version 0.5, in {appLanguages} languages: {appLanguageList}. It follows your system's language, or the one you choose in Settings → Language. The translations are new, so if a word is wrong, please tell us with Suggest a fix there.

items.q: Can I use my own sync server?
items.a: Yes. The sync server's code is public: submarine-sync-server on GitHub, with a guide for Docker or plain PHP hosting. In the app, open Cloud sync and change the sync server.

items.q: How do I delete my account?
items.a: In the app (version 0.5 and later), use Delete account… in Cloud sync. You can also do it on the delete account page.

items.q: How do I report a problem or ask for something?
items.a: From version 0.5, use Send feedback in Settings, or Feedback at the bottom of the profile list. It sends only what you type, and an email address only if you give one for an answer. You can also open an issue on GitHub.

security.title: How Submarine protects your data, and how to check it
security.description: What Submarine encrypts and how, what the sync server can and cannot see, what a hostile server could still do, and how to check each claim in the code.
security.heading: How your data is protected
security.lede: We don't ask you to trust us. This page explains exactly what is encrypted, what our server can and cannot see, and how you can check every claim yourself.
summary: Your servers, logins, keys and notes are kept in one file on your device, encrypted with AES-256-GCM. A few choices for this device only, such as the look of the app and a folder shared with an RDP server, are kept unencrypted in the app's settings and are never synced.
The key is made from your profile password with Argon2id, a method that is slow on purpose so that guessing is expensive. The password is never stored or sent anywhere.
If you turn on sync, each item is encrypted on your device before it is uploaded. The server stores data it cannot decrypt.

The server does see the outside of your data: your email address, when you sync and from which IP address, how many items of each kind you have and how big they are, your profile names, and for shared profiles the share names and the members' email addresses.

The AI assistant and AI agents are optional and off until you set them up. The assistant sends your messages, and what it reads on your servers, only to the AI provider you add, and only after you agree.
The app has no ads, no analytics and no crash reporting.

cannot: What is inside your items: names, addresses, ports, user names, passwords, private keys and their passphrases, tunnels, notes, commands, folder names
Which login or key belongs to which server
Your profile password, your sharing passphrase and the keys that open your profiles
can: Your email address, and your account password when you sign in (it stores only a bcrypt hash of it)
The IP address and time of sign-ins and syncs
How many items of each kind a profile has, their sizes, and when each one was changed and by which device (a random ID)
For shared profiles: the share names, the members' email addresses and their roles

diagram.stores: Stores encrypted items and the details listed above
diagram.caption: The password and the keys stay on your device. Only encrypted items, and the details around them, are sent.

sections.title: 1. On your device
paragraphs: Each profile is one file. Inside is a small database with your servers, logins, SSH keys, notes and settings. The whole database is compressed and then encrypted with AES-256-GCM. A new random nonce is used every time the file is saved, and the file is written to a temporary copy first, so a crash cannot leave half a file behind.

The key comes from your profile password through Argon2id with {argonMem} of memory, {argonPasses} passes and {argonLanes} lanes, and a random salt for each profile. These settings are fixed in the app, so a changed file cannot make them weaker.

The password is never written to disk and never sent anywhere. After the key is made, the copy of the password in the app's core is wiped, and the key is wiped when you lock the profile. Locking also closes every connection, and calls off a login that is still in progress. If you forget the password, the profile cannot be opened. There is no reset, because nothing that could open it is kept anywhere.

Quick unlock is optional and off by default. On Windows it uses Windows Hello and the TPM, on Android the fingerprint sensor and the Android Keystore. The system keeps the profile's key, never your password, and the key is never synced. On Android, the system's cloud backup of the app's data is turned off. Windows also has a separate switch, off by default, that opens a profile automatically: its key is then protected by Windows for your account, with no check at all, so anyone or any program using that Windows account can open it.

On Windows, when Remote Desktop Connection opens a server that has a saved password, the app hands the password over in a short-lived .rdp file. The password in it is encrypted with Windows DPAPI for your Windows user, and the file is deleted as soon as Remote Desktop Connection has read it (at the latest after 30 seconds; a file left behind by a crash is removed at the next start).

sections.title: 2. Cloud sync
paragraphs: Sync is off until you sign in. Each profile has its own random 256-bit data key, which lives inside the encrypted profile. Before upload, every item (a server, a login, a key, a note…) is encrypted on its own with this key, using AES-256-GCM and a new random nonce.

Next to each encrypted item, the server gets a random ID, the kind of item, a timestamp, and a flag that says whether it was deleted. The timestamp contains a random ID of the device that made the change. The size of the encrypted item shows roughly how big the item is. The server also stores each profile's name. Known host keys, command history, monitoring settings and the choices kept for this device only are never synced.

sections.title: 3. Opening a profile on a new device
paragraphs: To open a synced profile on another device, that device needs the profile's data key. So the server keeps one more record: the data key, encrypted with a key made from your profile password, with the same Argon2id settings. The server cannot open it.

This is also the main thing an attacker could try if they ever stole the server's data: guess your profile password offline. Every guess costs a full Argon2id run, so a long password that you use nowhere else keeps your data safe.

sections.title: 4. Your account password
paragraphs: Your sync account has its own password, separate from your profile password. It is sent to the server when you sign in, inside HTTPS, and the server stores only a bcrypt hash of it. After {lockoutTries} wrong passwords, password sign-in pauses for {lockoutMinutes} minutes.

The service sits behind Cloudflare, which handles the HTTPS connection for it. So, like the server, Cloudflare could see your account password when you sign in, but your items only in their encrypted form.
Never use your profile password as your account password. Then nothing the server or Cloudflare ever sees can open your profiles.

sections.title: 5. Sharing a profile
paragraphs: To share profiles, each account has an X25519 key pair. The private key is encrypted with a key made from your sharing passphrase (Argon2id again), and the passphrase never leaves your device. Each member of a shared profile gets the profile's data key sealed to their own public key.

When you invite someone, the app uses the public key that the server gives for that email address. If a member's key changes later, the app tells you and shows a fingerprint you can compare with them. The server knows the names of shared profiles and who is a member, but not what is inside.

sections.title: 6. If the server were hostile
paragraphs: Good security is not only about what a server is supposed to do. Here is what someone in full control of the server could and could not do.
cannot: Read your items, or change what is inside them without it being noticed
Open the stored copy of your profile key without your profile password
Learn your profile password or sharing passphrase, which the app never sends
Change the app on your device: there are no automatic updates, the app only shows that a new version exists
can: Try to guess a weak profile password offline, one slow Argon2id run per guess
Catch your account password the next time you sign in
Delete items, bring back older versions, or hold changes back. Before a sync deletes anything, the app keeps a copy of your profile on your device
Hand out the wrong public key when you invite someone to a shared profile
See the details listed in the table above

sections.title: 7. Everything the app connects to
paragraphs: Your own servers, and the proxies and jump hosts you set up for them. The sync server, only when you are signed in. Our server (submarine.sinaxhpm.com) when you send feedback, even if you sync with a server of your own, and then only with what you typed. The AI provider you add, while you use the AI assistant, and only after you agree to send it data. And GitHub, to check for a newer version: when the profile list opens and when you press “Check for updates”, the app asks GitHub's public list of releases. That request carries only the app's name and version. The iOS app, the Mac App Store version and the Flatpak never ask: their stores keep them up to date.

There is no analytics, crash reporting or advertising code in the app. The app trusts only its own built-in list of certificate authorities for sync, and it never follows a redirect, so it cannot be quietly pointed at another server.

sections.title: 8. What a remote desktop gets from your device
paragraphs: The clipboard. Text you paste into an RDP or VNC tab goes to that server, and nothing is offered to it before you paste. With Share the clipboard on (the default, and a switch for each server), text copied on the remote desktop is put on this device's clipboard. It is text only, never files, and VNC carries plain ASCII text only.

Files, only with the built-in RDP client on a computer, and only if you choose a folder or a drive for that server, read only if you like. The server sees it as a drive under \\tsclient, and nothing else of your computer. Every path it asks for is checked: no .., and no link is followed on the way, so nothing outside what you chose can be reached.
These choices are kept on this device and never synced, so nobody you share a profile with can turn them on.

sections.title: 9. The AI assistant and AI agents
paragraphs: Both are optional and off until you set them up. The assistant talks to the AI provider you add, straight from the app; nothing goes through a server of ours. Before the first message goes to a provider, the app asks, naming the address it goes to, and it sends that provider nothing until you agree. What goes there: your messages, and what the assistant reads on your servers to answer them (command output, file contents, folder listings). The provider's own terms cover what it does with them.

A private key in a command's output or in a file the assistant reads is replaced by a marker before anything is sent. The providers' API keys and your chats are kept in a file of their own next to the profile, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key made from the profile's key, so unlocking the profile opens them too. They stay on this device: they are never synced or exported.

The assistant goes only as far as the level you chose for the server. At the default level, Ask, a command runs by itself only when the app can tell from its text that it only reads, or when it is on the server's always-run list. Every other command, every change to a file, and reading a file that may hold secrets wait for your OK. Full access is never saved: it ends when the tab closes. Every file change is listed in Activity and can be undone there.

AI agents reach the running app only through a named pipe (Windows) or a Unix socket (macOS, Linux) that only your user account can open; there is no network port. An agent sees no server until you grant it one, it never gets a password or a key, and the server's address is replaced in everything it reads.

verify.title: Check it yourself
verify.lede: You don't have to take our word for any of this. Here are ways to check, from easy to advanced.

items.title: Read the code
items.text: The app is open source. The links on this page go to the exact lines that do the work, at the version this page describes ({commit}).

items.title: Watch the connections
items.text: Use a firewall or network monitor. You will see your own servers, the sync server only while you are signed in, submarine.sinaxhpm.com when you send feedback, api.github.com when the profile list opens (not in the App Store and Flatpak versions), and the AI provider you added while you use the assistant. Nothing else.

items.title: Look at what the server stores
items.text: Advanced: take your sign-in token from the app's data folder (cloud_token.json) and ask the API for your data, with the header X-Auth-Token: GET /api/sync/profiles, or POST /api/sync with an empty list of records. You get back only IDs, kinds, times, flags and encrypted text. Sign out in the app afterwards to end that session.

items.title: Read the traffic
items.text: Advanced: run a small proxy on your computer that passes requests on to the real server, and set the app's sync server to http://127.0.0.1 and the proxy's port. The app allows plain HTTP only for your own computer. You will see what the app sends, and that your items are encrypted. (A proxy certificate added to your system will not work, because the app uses its own list of certificate authorities.)

items.title: Decrypt your own data
items.text: Advanced: with your password, you can open your own data with any Argon2id and AES-GCM tool, using the settings in the table below. Without the password, nobody can.

items.title: Check your download
items.text: Compare the checksum with SHA256SUMS in the release (from version 0.5), check the Android app's certificate with apksigner, or build the app from source.

limits.title: What this page does not promise
items: Submarine has not had an independent security audit. Its reviews so far were done by the author.
A weak or reused password is the weakest point. Use a long, unique profile password, and a different account password.

Telnet and plain VNC are not encrypted by design. The app labels them, and can run them through an SSH server. Over plain VNC, clipboard text you paste or the server copies crosses the network unencrypted too.
The built-in RDP client is experimental (it is built from an IronRDP commit, not a release) and is off until you choose it for a server.
What the AI assistant sends to your provider is then covered by that provider's terms, not by this page. Don't use the assistant on servers whose data must not leave them.

privacy.title: Privacy policy – Submarine
privacy.description: What the Submarine app and its optional sync service keep, what they can and cannot read, how long it is kept, and how to delete it.
privacy.heading: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: This policy covers the Submarine app (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS), the optional Submarine sync service that the app can use, and this website.
short: Your servers, passwords, SSH keys and notes stay on your device, encrypted with a key made from your profile password. The app has no analytics, no advertising, no tracking and no crash reporting.
Cloud sync is optional. If you turn it on, the sync server keeps your account's email address and your profiles in encrypted form. It cannot read what is inside them.
You can delete your account, and everything the server holds for it, from inside the app or on this website.
A message you send with Send feedback reaches the developer with only what you typed in it.

The AI assistant is optional and does nothing until you add an AI provider with your own API key. Its chats go from your device to that provider, not to us. With a model on your own machine or network, they stay there.

sections.title: Who is responsible
paragraphs: Submarine is made by Sina Xhpm (sinaxhpm.com), who also runs the sync service at submarine.sinaxhpm.com (older versions of the app use api.sinaxhpm.com). The source code of the app is public at github.com/SinaXhpm/Submarine (MIT license), so what this policy says about the app can be checked in the code.

sections.title: What stays on your device
list: Your profiles (servers, logins, SSH keys, tunnels, notes, commands, known host keys, and passwords you choose to save from a login prompt) are stored in the app's data folder. They are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a key made from your profile password with Argon2id. The profile password is never stored and never sent anywhere. There is no way to recover it: if you forget it, the profile cannot be opened.

Quick unlock (optional, off by default): if you turn on Windows Hello or an Android fingerprint, the profile's key is sealed to a key held by the system (the TPM or the Android Keystore). The system checks your fingerprint or PIN; the app never sees it. On Windows you can instead choose to open a profile automatically (also off by default): its key is then protected by Windows for your account, with no check at all, so anyone or any program using that Windows account can open it.

The AI assistant's data (optional, see below): your AI providers and their API keys, your chats, the permission levels and always-run commands you set, and the assistant's activity log. They are kept in a file of their own beside the profile, encrypted with AES-256-GCM using a key made from the profile's key, so they open when the profile opens. This file is never synced, never part of a shared profile and never in an exported profile.

Settings such as the window position, the last-used profile name and the colour theme, and choices made for this device only (a remote desktop's speed and quality, whether it shares the clipboard, the folder or drive shared with an RDP server, and which servers always get a terminal with its own login) are stored in the app's own settings, not encrypted, and never synced.

The clipboard is read only when you paste. What you paste goes to the server you paste it into: a terminal, or a remote desktop's tab. With Share the clipboard on (the default for RDP and VNC servers), text copied on the remote desktop is put on this device's clipboard. Nothing from the clipboard is ever sent to us.

Remote Desktop Connection (Windows) gets a server's saved password in a short-lived .rdp file. The password in it is encrypted with Windows DPAPI for your Windows user, and the file is deleted once it has been read. If you let the RDP app remember a login itself, Windows keeps it, not Submarine.
The activity log in the app lives in memory and goes away when the app closes. The AI assistant keeps a log of its own (see below).

sections.title: What the app connects to
list: Your own servers. The app connects only to the hosts you add or open, using SSH, SFTP, FTP or FTPS, Telnet, VNC or RDP, through any proxy or jump host you set up. What you type and transfer goes to that server, not to us. For a remote desktop, that includes the clipboard text you paste into it, and a folder or drive of this computer if you choose to share one with the built-in RDP client. Plain FTP, plain Telnet and plain VNC are not encrypted, and the app says so.
The sync service, only if you sign in to cloud sync (see below). You can point the app at a server of your own instead; then that server's operator handles the data.

The AI providers you add, only if you use the AI assistant (see below). Requests go from your device straight to the provider, or through a proxy or one of your servers, as set for that provider. Submarine has no AI service of its own, and the sync service is not involved.

GitHub, to look for a newer version (not in the iOS app, the Mac App Store version or the Flatpak, which their stores keep up to date). When the profile list opens, and when you press “Check for updates”, the app asks GitHub's public list of releases (api.github.com) whether a newer version exists. The request carries the app's name and version (submarine-app/x.y.z) and nothing else; GitHub sees your IP address, as with any web request.
The developer's server, when you send feedback (see below), and only then.
Links you click open in your system browser.
sections.after: Nothing else leaves your device. The app contains no third-party analytics, advertising or tracking code.

table.title: Cloud sync (optional): what the sync server keeps
table.intro: If you create an account, the server stores:
head: What
Why
Can the server read it?
rows: Your email address
To sign you in, and to send sign-in and reset codes
Yes
Your account password
To sign you in
It receives the password over HTTPS when you sign in and stores only a salted bcrypt hash of it
Sign-in sessions: a hashed token, the IP address it was issued to, when it was last used, and an expiry ({sessionDays} days)
To keep you signed in
The token is hashed; the rest is readable
Your profiles' records
To sync them between your devices

No. Each record is encrypted on your device with the profile's key before it is uploaded. The server sees an ID for each record, its type (server, login, key, note…), timestamps (which include a random ID of the device that made the change), a deleted flag and the size, plus the profile's name and how many records it has
A copy of each profile's key, sealed with your profile password
To bring a profile onto a new device
Not without your profile password. Someone who got the server's data could try to guess a weak password offline, so use a long one
Sharing: your public key, your private key wrapped with your sharing passphrase, the names of shared profiles, the emails and roles of the people you share with, and the keys sealed to them
To share a profile with other accounts
The names and emails, yes; the keys, no

A log of account events: what happened (sign-up, sign-in, failed sign-in, sign-out, lock-out, password reset, a sync, a share invitation or change, and similar), the email address when it is known, the IP address, the time and Cloudflare's request ID. Never what was synced
To protect accounts and stop abuse
Yes. Kept for {auditDays} days, then deleted
Rate-limit counters, keyed by IP address and email
To slow down guessing and floods
Yes. Kept for {rateDays} days
after: Sign-ups that are never verified are deleted after {unverifiedDays} days.

The service sits behind Cloudflare, which handles the HTTPS connection for it and passes requests on to the server. So Cloudflare processes IP addresses, request headers and request contents, including your sign-in details and your already-encrypted records, on the service's behalf. The server sends verification and reset emails through its hosting provider's mail system.
We do not sell your data, share it with advertisers, use it for advertising, analytics or profiling, or combine it with anything else.

after.title: Feedback you send from the app
paragraphs: Send feedback (in Settings, on the profile list, and Suggest a fix under Language) sends a message to the developer. It is sent only when you press Send, and it contains only what you typed in the form: your message, a name if you give one, and an email address if you give one, used only to answer that message.

Nothing else is added: no logs, no list of your servers, no app version or system details, no account and no device ID. The message goes over HTTPS to the same server as cloud sync (submarine.sinaxhpm.com), also when you sync with a server of your own, and through Cloudflare like every request to it. The server uses your IP address against floods and does not keep it with the message: it goes into the rate-limit counters (kept for {rateDays} days) and, only if more messages than allowed come from it, into the log of account events (kept for {auditDays} days).

The developer reads the messages. They are kept for {feedbackDays} days and then deleted automatically; one can be deleted sooner on request. After sending, the app shows the message's report number: quote it to have that message deleted (see Contact). Messages are not shared with anyone and are not used for anything but reading and answering them.

after.title: AI assistant (optional)
paragraphs: The assistant does nothing until you add an AI provider in Settings → AI assistant: Anthropic, OpenAI, another OpenAI-compatible service (such as OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq or Google Gemini), or a model on your own machine or network (such as Ollama or LM Studio). You use your own account and API key with that provider, if it needs them. Submarine has no AI service of its own, and we never see your chats or your keys.
list: Where requests go. From your device straight to the provider, or through the system's proxy or one you set for it, or out through one of your servers over its open SSH session. Through a server, the provider sees that server's address. Requests use HTTPS, which stays encrypted from your device to the provider, so a proxy or server in between sees only which host is contacted and how much goes through. Plain http (not encrypted) is allowed only to an address on your own machine or network, or, through one of your servers, on that server's own machine or network. Over plain http, anyone on that network can read the chat and any API key sent with it, and on another network the same address can belong to someone else.

What the provider receives. The chat so far, with each request: your messages (with any terminal text you attach) and the assistant's replies. In a chat about a server, also what the assistant reads and does there (command output, file contents, folder listings, the results of its changes) and your answers when it asks for approval. The request carries your API key and the app's name and version, and, as with any web request, the provider sees the address it comes from. If you switch a chat to another provider, the whole chat goes to that one with your next message. Test and the requests that ask a provider about its models carry your key and nothing from your chats or servers.

Server facts. When a chat about a server starts, the app collects a few facts about the server and sends them with the chat: the system's short name and version number (as in debian 12), the kernel's name and version, the processor type, the login user's name and whether it is in an admin group (sudo, wheel or admin), the home folder, the name of the login shell, and which of bash, systemctl, docker, apt, dnf, yum, apk and pacman are installed. The chat shows them under Server facts sent to the assistant. They don't include the server's host name or address, or the name you gave it, though the assistant may come across these in what it reads.

Private keys. A private key block in command output (-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----, and the PGP, SSH2 and PuTTY forms) is replaced with [private key removed by Submarine] before it is shown or sent, and so is one in a file the assistant reads. This catches a key printed or read as a whole block; a command that prints only part of a key, or a key in another form, is not caught, so take it as a guard against accidents and not as a promise that no key can ever be sent. Other file contents, and terminal text you attach, are sent as they are, without hidden Unicode Tag characters: those can't be seen on screen and can carry instructions for a model, so they are taken out of everything the assistant is sent, your own messages included (the chat tells you when a message of yours held some). The assistant never gets the passwords and keys saved in your profile: it works only on the server, through the open session.

Your consent. What a provider receives is under that provider's own terms and privacy policy. Before your first message goes to a provider, the app asks you, naming the provider's address, and it asks again if you change that address to another host, change the provider's type, or allow providers that may keep data. An API key saved for one host is never sent to another: when you change the host, the app asks for the key again. For some providers it adds a note: Gemini (on Google's free tier, Google may use the data to improve its products, and people may read it), DeepSeek (it stores the data in China) and OpenRouter (it passes requests on to other providers; when it is added with the OpenRouter preset, Submarine asks it to use only ones that don't keep or train on data, unless you allow them in the provider's settings). To withdraw your consent, choose withdraw next to the provider in Settings → AI assistant: a chat that is answering stops before its next request, and the app asks again before the next message. What a provider already received stays under its own rules.
A local model (Ollama, LM Studio, or another server on your machine or network) keeps the data on that machine or network.

What is kept on your device: your providers and their API keys, your chats with everything in them, the permission level of each server and the commands you chose to always run there, and the assistant's activity log. The log lists each command the assistant ran or asked to run and each folder or file it opened or changed, with when it happened and whether and how it was allowed, and keeps the earlier content of each changed file so the change can be undone. Log entries older than 90 days are removed when the assistant's file is opened and each time a new entry is added. All of it is in the assistant's own encrypted file (see What stays on your device).

Report this reply (the flag under each reply) copies the reply to your clipboard and, once you confirm, opens the project's issue page on GitHub in your browser. The app sends nothing itself. What you post there is public, so leave out private data from your servers.

after.title: AI agents on this computer (optional)
paragraphs: On a computer, Settings → AI agents lets an AI agent that runs on the same computer (such as Claude Code) work on your servers through Submarine. It is off until you turn it on.
list: Who can connect. Only programs running as your user on this computer, through a channel that other users and the network can't open. Submarine shows you which program asks, and what started it.

Nothing without your approval. An agent asks for access, and you choose in Submarine's window the server, the operations, the folders, how long (8 hours at most) and how its operations run. Access ends when that time is up, when the agent disconnects, when you revoke it, lock the profile or close the app.

What an agent receives. The results of the operations you allow: command output, and folder listings and file contents from the folders you chose. Never your passwords, keys or other saved secrets. The address Submarine connects to is replaced in what the agent sees; other addresses a server prints can still appear.
Where it goes from there. What the agent does with what it receives, for example sending it to its own AI provider, is under that agent's terms and privacy policy.
What is kept on your device. Each operation an agent asks for is listed in the assistant's activity log, with the agent's name, on this device.

after.title: This website
paragraphs: This website uses no cookies, no analytics, no advertising and no third-party scripts or fonts. Like any website, Cloudflare and the hosting provider process your IP address, the page you ask for and your browser's details in order to deliver the page, and the hosting provider keeps standard server logs for a limited time.
If you delete your account on this website, what you type is sent only to the sync service, over HTTPS, and is not stored by the page.

after.title: Deleting your data
list: Delete your account in the app (version 0.5 and later): Cloud sync → (signed in) → Delete account…, or on the delete account page of this website. You confirm with your account password. This removes, at once: the cloud copies of all your profiles, your sharing key, every profile you shared (the people you shared it with lose access), your membership in other people's shares, your sessions, and the log entries of your account. Records you wrote into someone else's shared profile stay with that profile, with no writer named. Profiles on your devices are not touched.

Log lines written after that (the deletion itself, which carries no email, and any later sign-in attempt for that email) stay for up to {auditDays} days. Backups taken around updates of the server software are kept only briefly.
Remove one profile's cloud copy in the app: the profile's menu on the profile list, Delete from cloud….
Delete a feedback message before its {feedbackDays} days: contact us with its report number.

Delete the AI assistant's chats: one chat from its menu (Delete), or all of them with Delete all under the chat list on the AI page. The assistant's activity log outlives its chats unless you choose Clear them when you delete a chat; clear it any time with Clear the log in its Activity view, for one server or for every server. To delete a provider's API key, choose Remove next to the key in the provider's settings and save, or delete the provider, in Settings → AI assistant. Deleting a profile deletes the assistant's file with it. For what a provider received, its own rules apply: ask the provider.
Delete what is on a device by removing the app (for the Windows portable version, the folder next to the program).
If you use an older version, or can't open the app any more, contact us (below) and we will delete the account when you can show that it is yours.

after.title: Security
paragraphs: All traffic to the sync service uses HTTPS. Your profile password and your sharing passphrase never leave your device, and the keys that open your profiles are never stored on the server in a form it can open. The server limits sign-in attempts, pauses password sign-in for a while after repeated wrong passwords, and needs your password again for the most sensitive actions (replacing your sharing key, deleting your account). The security page explains all of this in detail.

after.title: Children
paragraphs: Submarine is a tool for system administrators and developers. It is not directed at children, and we do not knowingly collect data from them.

after.title: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: When this policy changes, the date at the top changes too. The full history of changes is in the repository.

after.title: Contact
paragraphs: Questions or requests about your data: write to {email}. You can also open an issue at github.com/SinaXhpm/Submarine/issues (please don't post private information there).

terms.title: Terms of use – Submarine
terms.description: The terms for the Submarine app and its optional sync service: the MIT license, your servers, fair use of your account, no warranty, and changes.
terms.heading: Terms of use
terms.intro: These terms cover the Submarine app, the optional Submarine sync service and this website. In short: the app is free and open source under the MIT license, the sync service is free and offered as it is, and you use both at your own risk and within the law. How we handle your data is in the privacy policy.

sections.title: Who we are
paragraphs: Submarine and its sync service are made and run by Sina Xhpm (sinaxhpm.com). “We” and “us” in these terms mean him.

sections.title: The app
paragraphs: The app is free and open source under the MIT license. You may use, copy, change and share it as that license allows. Nothing in these terms takes away a right the license gives you.
If you got the app through Apple's App Store or TestFlight, Apple's terms for those services also apply to that copy.

sections.title: Your servers, and what you do on them
list: Connect only to servers and devices that are yours, or that you are allowed to use.
You are responsible for what you do on them: the commands you run (also when you type into many servers at once), the files you change or delete, and the tunnels and shared folders you open.
Plain Telnet and plain VNC are not encrypted, and the app says so when a connection uses one of them.
Keep your own copies of anything important on your servers.

sections.title: The sync service and your account
list: Cloud sync is optional, and free within fair limits: {limitMb} MB of encrypted data, {limitItems} items and {limitProfiles} profiles per account.
You need an email address you can receive mail at. Sign-ups that are never verified are deleted after {unverifiedDays} days.
Keep your account password and your profile password safe. Your profiles are encrypted on your device, so we can't read them, and we can't recover a forgotten profile password.
You can point the app at a sync server of your own instead. These terms don't cover that server: its operator's rules do.

sections.title: Fair use of the sync service
paragraphs: The service is there to keep your own and your team's Submarine profiles in step. Please don't:
list: store or share anything you have no right to, or use the service against the law;
try to reach other people's accounts or data;
attack, overload or probe the service, or get around its limits;
make accounts in bulk, or with email addresses that aren't yours.
after: We may limit, suspend or delete an account that breaks these rules or harms the service or the people who use it. When we can, we tell you first by email.

sections.title: Deleting your account, and if the service ends
paragraphs: You can delete your account at any time: in the app (Delete account… in Cloud sync) or on the delete page. The privacy policy says what is deleted and when.

We may change the sync service, or stop it. Your profiles stay on your devices, encrypted, so stopping the service doesn't delete them there. If it ever stops, we'll say so on this website ahead of time, as early as we can.

sections.title: Feedback
paragraphs: We may use the ideas in feedback you send to improve Submarine. What a feedback message contains, and how long it is kept, is in the privacy policy.

sections.title: No warranty
paragraphs: The app and the sync service are provided “as is” and “as available”, without warranty of any kind, express or implied, including the implied warranties of merchantability, fitness for a particular purpose and non-infringement, as the MIT license says. We do our best to keep the service running and your data safe, but we don't promise that it will always be available, free of errors, or right for a particular purpose.

sections.title: Disclaimer of liability
paragraphs: You use the app and the sync service at your own risk. As far as the law allows, neither we nor anyone who has contributed to Submarine is liable for any loss or damage of any kind, direct or indirect, incidental, special or consequential, that comes from using the app and the sync service, from not being able to use them, or from relying on them. This includes, for example:
list: lost, damaged or leaked data, including profiles, keys and passwords;
anything done on servers and devices you connect to, whoever does it: you, the people you share a profile with, the AI assistant, or an AI agent you gave access;
lost access to a server, downtime, and lost work, business or profit;
what third parties do or keep, such as the servers you connect to, your AI providers, and network and hosting providers;
the sync service being unavailable, changed or ended.
after: Nothing in these terms limits a liability that the law does not allow to be limited, such as liability for intent or gross negligence, or for death or personal injury caused by negligence. Where the law of your country gives you rights that can't be waived, these terms don't take them away.

sections.title: Changes to these terms
paragraphs: When these terms change, the date at the top changes too. If a change matters for your account, we'll say so on this website. Using the app or the service after a change means you accept the new terms.

sections.title: Contact
paragraphs: Questions about these terms: write to {email}, or open an issue at github.com/SinaXhpm/Submarine/issues.

delete.heading: Delete your account
delete.lede: Deleting your sync account removes everything the server keeps for it, at once. It cannot be undone.
what: The cloud copies of all your profiles
Your sharing key, and every profile you shared (the people you shared it with lose access)
Your membership in other people's shared profiles
Your sessions, so you are signed out everywhere
The log entries of your account
stays: Profiles on your devices are not touched. To remove them, delete the profile in the app, or remove the app.
Records you wrote into someone else's shared profile stay with that profile, with no writer named.
Log lines written after the deletion (the deletion itself, without your email, and later sign-in attempts) are kept for up to {auditDays} days.
